# Exercise 3.1 — Supervised learning {#sec-supervised-learning}


:::: {.web-only}
Every cell on this page is a real R or Python cell. Open
`day3-01-supervised-learning.qmd` in your editor and run them one at a time —
the output printed here is what you should get.
::::

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Say what the learning algorithm, the fitted model and the dataset each
  contribute to a prediction, pointing at one line of code for each.
- Fit the same model in both languages, read its two parameters, and predict a
  value both inside and outside the range of the data.
- Swap the learning algorithm for a decision tree without changing anything
  else, and describe how the shape of the prediction changes.
:::

## Why this, here

In @sec-pipeline you fitted a model with one call and read a score off the test
set. The fitting itself was a black box: `fit()` went in, coefficients came out.
Today we open it. This exercise sets up the pieces — data, algorithm, fitted
parameters, prediction — so that @sec-loss-functions can ask what "best fit"
means and @sec-gradient-descent can ask how the best fit is found.

## The data we fit to

Today's outcome is a blood glucose measurement and the single predictor is age.
The question behind it: **does knowing a patient's age tell you anything useful
about their glucose?** The answer today is more interesting than you might
expect.

`data/diabetes.csv` is the module's case study: 768 adults screened for type 2
diabetes, eight measurements from a single visit and a `pos`/`neg` outcome. It
carries the defect you met on Day 2 — five rows record a glucose of 0, which is
not a measurement — so we drop those rows and keep the first 80 of what is left,
small enough to see every point on a scatter plot.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2)

diab <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu  <- diab |> filter(glucose > 0) |> slice(1:80) |> select(age, glucose)

nrow(glu)
head(glu)
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

diab = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
glu = (diab.loc[diab["glucose"] > 0, ["age", "glucose"]]
           .head(80)
           .reset_index(drop=True))

len(glu), glu.head()
```
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
ggplot(glu, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Age in years (the feature)",
       y = "Glucose, mg/dL (the label)")
```

## Python

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Age in years (the feature)")
ax.set_ylabel("Glucose, mg/dL (the label)")
plt.show()
```
:::

Look at the scatter before you fit anything, and write down what slope you
expect. You will be asked for it again at the end.

## The three things that make a prediction

| | What it is | In the code below |
|---|---|---|
| The **learning algorithm** | a procedure for turning data into parameters | `linear_reg()`, `LinearRegression()` |
| The **fitted model** | the parameters it produced, and nothing else | $\hat\beta_0 = 110.30$, $\hat\beta_1 = 0.289$ |
| The **dataset** | what the algorithm was allowed to see | the 80 rows in `glu` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,44,32]"}

The algorithm is chosen by you, the parameters are chosen by the data, and the
prediction is a consequence of both. Students conflate the first two constantly:
"linear regression predicted 123" is wrong, because linear regression predicts
nothing until it has been shown a dataset.

In machine learning notation the model is written

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1$$

where $y$ is the label (glucose), $x_1$ the feature (age), $\beta_0$ the
intercept — often called the bias — and $\beta_1$ the weight on the feature,
which is the slope. Both are *parameters*: numbers the fitting procedure
returns.

## Fitting, in both languages

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(parsnip)

lm_model <- linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm") |> set_mode("regression")
ls_fit   <- lm_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

coef(extract_fit_engine(ls_fit))
```

## Python

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = glu[["age"]]      # 2-D: a frame, not a series
y = glu["glucose"]    # 1-D
lin_reg = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)

lin_reg.intercept_, lin_reg.coef_[0]
```
:::

The two agree to every decimal worth printing, because both solve the same
least-squares problem on the same 80 rows. @sec-ols shows you the algebra they
are solving and verifies it by hand.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `coef()` does not work on a parsnip fit
`coef(ls_fit)` returns `NULL` — silently, with no error. A `model_fit` object
wraps the engine's fit rather than being one, so you have to reach inside with
`extract_fit_engine()` first. Passing the `NULL` to `geom_abline()` then fails
some distance from the line that caused it, which is the most annoying class of
bug there is.
:::

So the fitted model is

$$\widehat{\text{glucose}} = 110.30 + 0.289 \times \text{age}$$

and that is the entire deliverable of the fitting step. Two numbers.

## Predicting, inside and outside the data

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
new_patients <- data.frame(age = c(45, 10))
predict(ls_fit, new_data = new_patients)
```

## Python

```{python}
lin_reg.predict(pd.DataFrame({"age": [45, 10]}))
```
:::

A 45-year-old gets a predicted glucose of about 123.3. So does a 10-year-old,
at about 113.2 — even though the youngest patient in the data is 21, and these
are adults with no children among them. The model is an infinite line. It will
return a number for an age of 200, or of −40, and nothing in the code will
object.

::: {.callout-note}
## Extrapolation is a modelling decision, not a software error
The line is fitted on ages 21 to 81. Using it at 10 asserts that the same
relationship holds in children, which nothing in these data supports. Every
model will happily extrapolate; the restraint has to come from you. Note also
what the model does *not* give you: any sense of how confident it is. That is a
statistical question and this is a prediction course.
:::

## Task 1 — Predict from the parameters, not from the function

`predict()` is a convenience. Reproduce it with arithmetic: compute the
predicted glucose for a 60-year-old from the two coefficients.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
b <- coef(extract_fit_engine(ls_fit))
pred_60 <- ______ + ______ * 60
check_metric_range(pred_60, 120, 135, "predicted glucose at age 60")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")
b <- coef(extract_fit_engine(ls_fit))
pred_60 <- b[1] + b[2] * 60
check_metric_range(pred_60, 120, 135, "predicted glucose at age 60")
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
pred_60 = ______ + ______ * 60
check_metric_range(pred_60, 120, 135, "predicted glucose at age 60")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
pred_60 = lin_reg.intercept_ + lin_reg.coef_[0] * 60
check_metric_range(pred_60, 120, 135, "predicted glucose at age 60")
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The two numbers you need are the ones the fitting step printed. In R they come
out of `coef()` in the order intercept, then slope; in Python they are two
separate attributes of the fitted object.
:::

## Task 2 — Make the line earn its place

A fitted line is only worth having if it beats a predictor that does no
learning. Compute the mean squared error of the line on these 80 rows, and the
mean squared error of predicting the mean glucose for everybody.

Both numbers are computed on the rows the model was fitted to, which
@sec-pipeline told you is not evidence of anything. Today that is deliberate:
this exercise is about what fitting *does*, not about how well it generalises.
Read every number on this page as in-sample.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
pred_line <- predict(ls_fit, new_data = glu)$.pred
mse_line  <- mean((glu$glucose - ______)^2)
mse_mean  <- mean((glu$glucose - ______)^2)
check_beats_baseline(mse_line, mse_mean)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")
pred_line <- predict(ls_fit, new_data = glu)$.pred
mse_line  <- mean((glu$glucose - pred_line)^2)
mse_mean  <- mean((glu$glucose - mean(glu$glucose))^2)
check_beats_baseline(mse_line, mse_mean)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
mse_line = np.mean((y - ______)**2)
mse_mean = np.mean((y - ______)**2)
check_beats_baseline(mse_line, mse_mean)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
mse_line = np.mean((y - lin_reg.predict(X))**2)
mse_mean = np.mean((y - y.mean())**2)
check_beats_baseline(mse_line, mse_mean)
```
:::
:::
:::

The check prints the line's error as a percentage of the baseline's. Write the
percentage down before you read the next section.

## The result that should bother you

The line's in-sample mean squared error is 847.5. The mean squared error of
ignoring age entirely and predicting 119.9 for everyone is 863.2. Fitting
removed 1.8% of the squared error.

Now destroy the relationship on purpose and fit again. Shuffling the age column
breaks any link between a patient's age and their glucose while leaving both
distributions exactly as they were.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
set.seed(42)
glu_shuffled <- glu |> mutate(age = sample(age))

fit_shuffled  <- lm_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu_shuffled)
pred_shuffled <- predict(fit_shuffled, new_data = glu_shuffled)$.pred

coef(extract_fit_engine(fit_shuffled))
mean((glu_shuffled$glucose - pred_shuffled)^2)
```

## Python

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
glu_shuffled = glu.assign(age=rng.permutation(glu["age"].values))

fit_shuffled = LinearRegression().fit(glu_shuffled[["age"]], glu_shuffled["glucose"])
mse_shuffled = np.mean((glu_shuffled["glucose"]
                        - fit_shuffled.predict(glu_shuffled[["age"]]))**2)

fit_shuffled.intercept_, fit_shuffled.coef_[0], mse_shuffled
```
:::

Three steps of reasoning.

1. Shuffled age cannot predict glucose. Any apparent fit is coincidence, and
   its error is what "no relationship at all" looks like in these units.
2. The shuffled fit's error is around 850 in R and around 861 in Python — the
   two seeds shuffle differently — against 847.5 for the real age column and
   863.2 for the baseline. The real predictor buys you almost nothing that a
   deliberately broken one does not.
3. The algebra in @sec-ols is exact, the fit is genuinely the best straight
   line there is, and the model is still not worth deploying. A minimum is not
   the same thing as a small number.

Keep this: the entire day is about finding the best line, and the best line
here is nearly useless. Being able to hold both of those at once is the point.

## Task 3 — Change the algorithm, keep everything else

A decision tree is a different learning algorithm applied to the identical
dataset and the identical question. You meet trees properly on Day 5; for
now, swap one line and look at the shape of what comes out.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)

dt_model <- decision_tree(mode = "regression") |> set_engine("______")
dt_fit   <- dt_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

rpart.plot(extract_fit_engine(dt_fit), roundint = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The engine is the package that does the work, exactly as `"lm"` was for
`linear_reg()`. For trees in R it is the recursive-partitioning package, and
the string is its name.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)

dt_model <- decision_tree(mode = "regression") |> set_engine("rpart")
dt_fit   <- dt_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

rpart.plot(extract_fit_engine(dt_fit), roundint = FALSE)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, export_text

tree_reg = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5).fit(______, ______)
print(export_text(tree_reg, feature_names=["age"]))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The tree takes the same two arguments the linear model took, in the same order.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, export_text

tree_reg = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5).fit(X, y)
print(export_text(tree_reg, feature_names=["age"]))
```
:::
:::
:::

Now plot both models' predictions over the data. The line is a line; the tree is
a staircase, constant within each age band it chose.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
dt_fit_shown <- decision_tree(mode = "regression") |> set_engine("rpart") |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

glu_pred <- glu |>
  mutate(pred_tree = predict(dt_fit_shown, new_data = glu)$.pred,
         pred_line = predict(ls_fit,       new_data = glu)$.pred)

ggplot(glu_pred, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = glucose), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_step(aes(y = pred_tree), colour = "darkred", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred_line), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)")
```

## Python

```{python}
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
tree_shown = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5).fit(X, y)

grid = pd.DataFrame({"age": np.linspace(glu["age"].min(), glu["age"].max(), 400)})
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=0.5)
ax.plot(grid["age"], tree_shown.predict(grid), color="darkred")
ax.plot(grid["age"], lin_reg.predict(grid), color="steelblue")
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)"); ax.set_ylabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
plt.show()
```
:::

The tree's in-sample mean squared error is lower than the line's: 685.7 in R
with `rpart`'s default pruning, 677.9 in Python with a depth of 3. Both are well
below the line's 847.5. The tree is not better. It has more parameters — one
mean per leaf rather than two numbers for the whole dataset — and more
parameters always fit the rows you fitted them to more closely. Day 5 is
where that argument gets settled.

::: {.callout-note}
## The two trees are not the same tree
`rpart` and scikit-learn choose splits the same way but stop differently:
`rpart` prunes using a complexity parameter and cross-validation, scikit-learn
stops when you tell it to. Ours end up with six leaves and seven respectively.
Unlike the linear coefficients, which agreed to the decimal, the trees are a
genuine difference between the two libraries' defaults, and you should expect to
have to state tree-stopping rules explicitly whenever you report one.
:::

## Task 4 — The role of the dataset

Refit both models on the first 30 rows only, and predict glucose for a
25-year-old with each of the four fitted models.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
glu30 <- glu |> slice(______)

ls_fit30 <- lm_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = ______)
dt_fit30 <- decision_tree(mode = "regression") |> set_engine("rpart") |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = ______)

at25 <- data.frame(age = 25)
c(line80 = predict(ls_fit,   at25)$.pred, line30 = predict(ls_fit30, at25)$.pred,

```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer

```{r}
glu30 <- glu |> slice(1:30)

ls_fit30 <- lm_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu30)
dt_fit30 <- decision_tree(mode = "regression") |> set_engine("rpart") |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = glu30)

at25 <- data.frame(age = 25)
c(line80 = predict(ls_fit,   at25)$.pred, line30 = predict(ls_fit30, at25)$.pred,
  tree80 = predict(dt_fit_shown, at25)$.pred, tree30 = predict(dt_fit30, at25)$.pred)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
glu30 = glu.head(______)
X30, y30 = glu30[["age"]], glu30["glucose"]

lin30  = LinearRegression().fit(______, ______)
tree30 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5).fit(______, ______)

at25 = pd.DataFrame({"age": [25]})
{"line80": lin_reg.predict(at25)[0],   "line30": lin30.predict(at25)[0],
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}

## Worked answer
```{python}
glu30 = glu.head(30)
X30, y30 = glu30[["age"]], glu30["glucose"]

lin30  = LinearRegression().fit(X30, y30)
tree30 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5).fit(X30, y30)

at25 = pd.DataFrame({"age": [25]})
{"line80": lin_reg.predict(at25)[0],   "line30": lin30.predict(at25)[0],
 "tree80": tree_shown.predict(at25)[0], "tree30": tree30.predict(at25)[0]}
```
:::
:::
:::

Answer in writing, in one sentence each.

1. Which model's prediction for a 25-year-old moved more when 50 rows were
   taken away, and by how much?
2. The learning algorithm did not change between the two fits. What did?
3. On 30 rows the `rpart` tree has two leaves rather than six. What has the
   algorithm concluded, and is it wrong to conclude it?

## Reflection

1. A colleague says "the model says glucose rises by 0.29 mg/dL per year of
   age". Rewrite that sentence so it is defensible, given everything on this
   page.
2. You chose linear regression before seeing the data and the tree after. Which
   of the two decisions is more dangerous, and why?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** Task 4: the line at age 25 moves from 117.5 to 105.1, the tree from
116.4 to 95.7 — the tree moves roughly twice as far, because each leaf is a mean
over a handful of patients while the line pools all of them. What changed is the
dataset, and only the dataset; this is the whole lesson of the exercise. The
two-leaf tree on 30 rows has concluded, correctly for those rows, that there is
only enough evidence for one split; `rpart`'s pruning is doing its job.
Reflection 1 wants three repairs: *predicted* rather than *rises*, no causal
verb at all, and the in-sample caveat. Reflection 2: choosing the tree after
seeing the data is the dangerous one, and Day 5 shows why.

**Expected values** (regenerated data varies in the last digit). Coefficients
≈ 110.3 and ≈ 0.29. In-sample MSE: line ≈ 845–850, predict-the-mean ≈ 860–865,
`rpart` tree ≈ 680–690, scikit-learn depth-3 tree ≈ 675–680. Shuffled-age MSE
≈ 845–865 depending on the language's generator. Predictions at age 25:
line ≈ 117, line on 30 rows ≈ 105, tree ≈ 116, tree on 30 rows ≈ 96.

**Common failures.** (1) `coef(ls_fit)` returning `NULL`, which the callout
pre-empts but students still hit — the error surfaces inside `geom_abline()`.
(2) In Python, `glu["age"]` instead of `glu[["age"]]`, giving a shape error.
(3) Reading the 1.8% improvement as "the model is broken" rather than "age does
not predict glucose here"; the data is behaving, the predictor is weak.

**Plenary.** Ask for the slope people wrote down from the scatter plot before
fitting. Most will have guessed something steeper than 0.29. That gap is the
reason we measure.

**Timing.** Tasks 1 and 2 are quick. Protect twenty minutes for Tasks 3 and 4
together; if you are short, drop the Python tab of Task 4 and do it in plenary.
:::
:::

Refit the line with `mass` (body mass index) as the predictor instead of age,
on the same 80 rows, and compare the in-sample MSE with the baseline. Then ask
the question this exercise cannot: is the comparison between the two predictors
fair, given that you chose the second one after seeing the first one fail?
:::

## Stretch 2 — All 763 rows
Repeat the fit on every row with a non-zero glucose rather than the first 80.
The slope roughly doubles, to about 0.52, and the scatter looks no more
convincing. Which of the two slopes would you report, and what does your answer
imply about reporting a coefficient from a subset at all?
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can fit, read and apply a two-parameter model in both
languages, swap the learning algorithm without touching anything else, and
state what the dataset contributed to the result.

**Cannot:** that this line is the best one. We never defined "best" — we used
whatever `lm()` optimises, which happens to be squared error. That choice does
real work, and it is @sec-loss-functions.
